title: Spooky action
subtitle: Create entangled pairs and see why Einstein was bothered — and why nothing travels faster than light anyway.

steps.title: Two qubits, one state
body: In 1935, Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen published a paper pointing out a strange consequence of quantum mechanics: particles that have interacted can end up with perfectly linked measurement results, even very far apart.
Einstein later called this “spooky action at a distance”. He suspected the theory was incomplete.
Today we know, from experiments, that entanglement is real. And you're going to create it with two gates.

steps.title: Create a Bell pair
steps.goal: Reach (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2: both qubits always equal, but each one random.
hints: Put the first qubit in superposition.
Then the CNOT: select it and click the control wire (●). With two qubits, the other wire becomes the target (⊕).
steps.success: Look at the spheres: the arrows shrank to the center. Entangled, neither has a state of its own — the state belongs to the pair.

steps.title: Alice and Bob measure
steps.body: Imagine Alice and Bob a galaxy apart, each with one qubit of the pair. Measure several times.
steps.after: Always equal: 00 or 11. But notice that, for Alice alone, the result is a fair coin. The correlation only shows up when the two compare notes.

steps.question: Alice measures and gets 1. She knows right away that Bob will get 1. Can this be used to send a message faster than light?

options.text: Yes: Alice picks the result and Bob reads it.
options.why: Alice doesn't pick anything — her result is random. She has no way to encode a message in it.

options.text: No: the results are random, and the correlation only shows up when comparing data over an ordinary channel.
options.why: Exactly. It's called the no-signaling theorem. Entanglement is a correlation, not a telephone.

options.text: Yes, but only with many pairs.
options.why: Not even with many: Bob's local statistics are always 50/50, whatever Alice does.

steps.title: Inseparable opposites
hints: Start with the Bell pair you already know how to make. Then flip one side.
steps.success: A different Bell state, with perfect anticorrelation. There are four Bell states, and they all turn into one another with single-qubit gates.

steps.title: Three at once (GHZ)
hints: Make a Bell pair and then “extend” the chain with one more CNOT.
steps.success: A GHZ state (Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger). Measuring any one of the three reveals the other two.

steps.title: Entanglement from space
steps.text: In 2017, the Chinese satellite Micius sent pairs of entangled photons to two ground stations about 1,200 km apart. The correlations survived the trip.

steps.title: Einstein was wrong (this time)
steps.text: In 1964, John Bell showed it's possible to test whether entanglement hides prior “instructions”. Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger did the experiments — and nature violated Bell's inequalities. Nobel Prize in Physics 2022.

takeaways: H followed by CNOT creates a Bell pair: two qubits with perfectly correlated results.
When entangled, qubits have no individual state — on the sphere, the arrows shrink.
Correlation isn't communication: nothing travels faster than light.
